title: Wi-Fi router or modem: safe teardown
summary: A working router is worth keeping whole for a local network. A dead one gives a 12 V adapter (usually), Wi-Fi antennas and coax, Ethernet and power jacks, heatsinks and LEDs. Low risk, except travel routers with lithium batteries and wall-plug units with a mains supply inside.

steps.text: Unplug the adapter from the wall, then from the router, and pull out every other cable too (Ethernet, coax or phone line, USB): a PoE unit gets its power through the Ethernet cable. Keep them together and read the adapter label: output volts, amps and the polarity symbol. Write it on the router with a marker if the label is worn.

Check whether it has a built-in or backup battery: pocket travel routers and mobile hotspots often do, and some modems have a backup battery bay. If the case bulges or creaks, stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium.
steps.warn: Never pry open a bulging case or press on a swollen battery. A punctured lithium cell can catch fire within seconds.

steps.text: Check whether the mains plug pins are built into the case (wall-plug extenders and some travel routers). If so, there is a small mains supply inside: leave it unplugged at least 5 minutes before opening.
steps.warn: Inside a wall-plug unit, the supply board can hold a charge for days. Don't open it before it has been unplugged for 5 minutes, and don't touch the board until you have discharged it (see safety_discharge_capacitor).

steps.text: Unscrew any external antennas by their ribbed base, turning anticlockwise.
Find the case screws. Peel up the rubber feet and press around labels for hidden holes. Undo them; many need a small Phillips bit (#0 on the Archer C7) or a Torx bit (T6 on the Velop).
Work a plastic pry tool or an old plastic card along the seam to pop the clips, then lift the cover off. Note any clip that hooks the other way and release it from the other side.
steps.warn: Metal blades crack the plastic clips and can slip into your hand. On a unit with a battery, keep the tool shallow and work along the seam: the battery can sit right behind the cover, and a puncture can start a fire.

steps.text: Wall-plug units and any unit with a mains supply board inside: do this before you touch anything. Find the largest capacitors (tall cylinders near the mains pins, often rated 200 V or more). Drain each one through your resistor tool, holding the probe on each terminal for 10 seconds. Then set the meter to DC volts and measure across each capacitor and from each to the metal shield: it must read under 1 V. Leave a jumper across it while you work (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
Battery units: unplug the battery by its plastic plug, never by the wires, and tape over the plug. Lift the battery out with your fingers or a plastic card, not a metal tool.
steps.warn: If you must cut battery wires, cut one at a time and tape each end before cutting the next. Never let the bare ends touch.

steps.text: Unplug the internal antenna leads: lift each tiny round connector straight up off the board with a spudger or fingernail. Peel stick-on antennas off the inside of the case and keep their thin coax attached.
steps.warn: These connectors are fragile. Pull straight up from the connector body, never by the thin cable.

steps.text: Undo the screws holding the board and lift it out. If a heatsink is stuck on with a soft thermal pad, twist it gently side to side until it lets go.
Desolder the parts you want: the DC power jack, Ethernet jacks, USB sockets and status LEDs (see skill_soldering). Leave the metal-shielded radio section and the chips on the board.

Test the adapter only if its case, cord and plug are undamaged; never plug in a cracked or cut one. Set the meter to DC volts with the leads in the COM and V sockets, plug the adapter into mains, and measure between the centre of the plug and its outer sleeve, holding the probes by their handles. Expect the label voltage or a little above with nothing connected. Unplug it before you put it away.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The whole router, if it works.** Even with no internet it makes a local Wi-Fi network, so phones and laptops nearby can share files and messages. Keep a working one whole. The OpenWrt Table of Hardware lists which models can run OpenWrt, free router software with far more settings than the maker's (OpenWrt ToH). Most run from a 12 V adapter, so they can be run from a 12 V battery too (see build_dc_ups_router). Netgear says its routers never draw more than their adapter's rating; the R7000's adapter is rated 12 V 3.5 A (Netgear KB 23003).
- **The adapter.** A regulated low-voltage DC supply, usually 12 V. Good for 12 V LED lights, radios and small fans where mains or a generator exists. Check volts, amps and polarity on the label.
- **Antennas and their coax.** Detachable antennas screw on with RP-SMA connectors; internal ones are thin wires or stick-on boards with a short coax lead and a tiny snap-on plug. The TP-Link Archer C7 v2 has three detachable 5 GHz antennas rated 5 dBi and three internal 2.4 GHz ones (TP-Link Archer C7 V2 UG). Use them as spares for other Wi-Fi gear. They are cut for 2.4 or 5 GHz and are a poor match for LoRa or walkie-talkie bands (see reference_lora_bands).
- **Connectors.** Ethernet jacks, the DC barrel jack and USB sockets, for repairs and your own builds.
- **Heatsinks.** Small aluminium heatsinks, some with thermal pads (iFixit Velop), for voltage regulators and LED drivers you build.
- **Status LEDs.** Small indicator LEDs, useful as power lights on your own builds.
- **Built-in battery** (travel routers only). A small lithium pack. Store and handle it as safety_swollen_lithium describes.

## Variations

The 682 routers logged here from the OpenWrt Table of Hardware give a rough picture (OpenWrt ToH). They were imported, not checked one by one, so read your own labels.

- **Adapter voltage.** Of 671 entries with a power supply, 444 use 12 V, 80 use 5 V (some by USB), 46 use 9 V, 30 use 24 V, 19 use 19 V and 14 use 48 V. About 116 mention PoE: access points and outdoor units powered through the Ethernet cable, sometimes at 24 V or 48 V. Netgear's own list shows 12 V and 19 V adapters (Netgear KB 23003).
- **Mains inside.** About 9 list a mains input (100 to 240 V AC, or 230 V) instead of a DC adapter, which points to a wall-plug unit with a small mains supply in the case.
- **Batteries.** 6 are travel routers or hotspots with a built-in lithium battery of 2,000 to 6,400 mAh. Some modems have a backup battery too, and TP-Link's setup guide says to remove it (TP-Link Archer C7 V2 UG).
- **Antennas.** About 200 list detachable external antennas; the rest have internal ones. Mesh units hide all their antennas inside, and their antenna plugs are fragile (iFixit Velop).
- **Cases.** Some open with four screws and a ring of clips, with the antennas unscrewing from the outside (iFixit Archer C7). Others hide screws under rubber feet and need Torx T6 (iFixit Velop).
- **Cable modems.** Some are plain modems: the Arris SB8200 is a cable modem with one coax F connector and two Ethernet jacks (Arris SB8200). They give less: the adapter, jacks and connectors.
- **Hardware versions.** One model name can hide different insides: the OpenWrt table gives each hardware version (v1, v2 and so on) its own entry (OpenWrt ToH). Read the version on the label.

## What to leave

- **Radio chips, processor and memory.** Soldered under metal shields, and of no use off the board.
- **On-board buck converters.** The small regulators that make 1 to 5 V for the chips are built into the board. Buy or salvage a separate buck board instead.
- **The plastic case**, unless you need small project boxes.

## Testing what you got out

- **Adapter.** As in the last step: the label voltage or a little above, unloaded. A reading of zero or far below means it is dead.
- **LEDs.** Touch the legs to a 3 V coin cell: a good LED lights one way round and not the other. On a meter's diode setting a good LED may glow faintly, though some meters can't light white or blue ones.
- **Antennas and coax.** Look for crushed or kinked coax and loose connectors. A meter can't tell you much about antenna quality; try it on working gear.
